178	impl RunGrade {
179	    /// Grade a run from its time-ordered batch summaries; `None`
180	    /// when the run produced no batches (nothing to grade).
181	    ///
182	    /// - Both floor signals read `floor_q_ps`, the batch's robust
183	    ///   low-quantile floor, never its raw min — see
184	    ///   [`crate::harness::BATCH_FLOOR_Q`] for the measurement
185	    ///   that settled it.
186	    /// - `drift` compares the median floor of the run's first
187	    ///   quarter against its last: the plain end-to-end question,
188	    ///   did the run finish where it started. Movement is
189	    ///   reported, not attributed — see the module doc.
190	    /// - `step` is the transition detector — the split point that
191	    ///   most divides the floor series, scored on the medians of
192	    ///   the two sides. A run that shifts and shifts back reads
193	    ///   low on drift and high on step; the reported time says
194	    ///   when it happened.
195	    /// - Both are medians, not extremes, on purpose: a single hot
196	    ///   batch is a burst, not a transition, and an adjacent-pair
197	    ///   detector graded every quiet 3900X run D/F on exactly
198	    ///   those isolated batches.
199	    /// - Runs shorter than [`MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES`] batches per side
200	    ///   score 0 on both — too few floors to say anything.
201	    pub fn from_batches(batches: &[BatchSummary]) -> Option<Self> {
202	        if batches.is_empty() {
203	            return None;
204	        }
205	
206	        let total: u64 = batches.iter().map(|b| b.count).sum();
207	        let over: u64 = batches.iter().map(|b| b.over_floor).sum();
208	        let interference_frac = if total == 0 {
209	            0.0
210	        } else {
211	            over as f64 / total as f64
212	        };
213	
214	        let means: Vec<f64> = batches.iter().map(|b| b.mean_ps).collect();
215	        let typical = median(&means).unwrap_or(0.0); // OK: `batches` is non-empty
216	        let hot = means
217	            .iter()
218	            .filter(|&&m| m > typical * (1.0 + BURST_TOL))
219	            .count();
220	        let burst_frac = hot as f64 / batches.len() as f64;
221	
222	        let floors: Vec<f64> = batches.iter().map(|b| b.floor_q_ps as f64).collect();
223	        let n = floors.len();
224	
225	        let quarter = (n / 4).max(1);
226	        let drift_frac = split_change(&floors[..quarter], &floors[n - quarter..]);
227	
228	        let times: Vec<f64> = batches.iter().map(|b| b.t_start_s).collect();
229	        let (step_frac, step_at_s) = best_split(&floors, &times);
230	
231	        let mut grade = Self {
232	            interference_frac,
233	            burst_frac,
234	            drift_frac,
235	            step_frac,
236	            step_at_s,
237	            letter: 'A',
238	        };
239	        grade.letter = score_letter(grade.scores().into_iter().fold(0, u8::max));
240	        Some(grade)
241	    }
242	
243	    /// Per-signal scores in print order: interference, bursts,
244	    /// drift, step.
245	    ///
246	    /// Each is the count of its [`thresholds`] cutoffs crossed —
247	    /// 0 (below all four) through 4 — and the composite is
248	    /// `fold(0, u8::max)` over them: the worst signal wins
249	    /// outright, so one F makes the letter F and no number of
250	    /// A's pulls it back. Printing every signal's letter beside
251	    /// the composite makes that visible: the overall letter is
252	    /// always one of the four shown.
253	    fn scores(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
254	        [
255	            score(self.interference_frac, thresholds::INTERFERENCE),
256	            score(self.burst_frac, thresholds::BURSTS),
257	            score(self.drift_frac, thresholds::DRIFT),
258	            score(self.step_frac, thresholds::STEP),
259	        ]
260	    }
261	
262	    /// Letters for the gauge line's printed signals, in print
263	    /// order — all four composite inputs, so the worst letter on
264	    /// the line *is* the composite.
265	    pub fn signal_letters(&self) -> [char; 4] {
266	        self.scores().map(score_letter)
267	    }
268	}

270	/// The transition detector, shared by both grades: the split
271	/// point that most divides a floor series, returned as
272	/// `(relative change, time of the split)`.
273	///
274	/// - Scans every interior split keeping [`MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES`] on
275	///   each side, scoring each on the medians of the two sides. `n`
276	///   is a batch or probe count (tens), so the O(n^2 log n) scan
277	///   costs microseconds against a run's seconds.
278	/// - Ranked by change x the split's balance, `n1 * n2 / n^2`: a
279	///   floor series has a plateau of splits reading the same change
280	///   (any cut inside the earlier level sees the same two
281	///   medians), and the balance term picks the one nearest the
282	///   middle of that plateau — the transition itself — instead of
283	///   whichever tie came first.
284	/// - Series with fewer than `2 * MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES` points score
285	///   0 at the first timestamp: too few floors to say anything.
286	/// - `floors` and `times` are parallel; a short `times` only
287	///   costs the reported timestamp, never the change.
288	fn best_split(floors: &[f64], times: &[f64]) -> (f64, f64) {
289	    let n = floors.len();
290	    let mut step_frac = 0.0f64;
291	    let mut step_at_s = times.first().copied().unwrap_or(0.0);
292	    let mut best_rank = 0.0f64;
293	    if n >= 2 * MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES {
294	        for t in MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES..=(n - MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES) {
295	            let change = split_change(&floors[..t], &floors[t..]);
296	            let balance = (t * (n - t)) as f64 / (n * n) as f64;
297	            let rank = change * balance;
298	            if rank > best_rank {
299	                best_rank = rank;
300	                step_frac = change;
301	                step_at_s = times.get(t).copied().unwrap_or(step_at_s);
302	            }
303	        }
304	    }
305	    (step_frac, step_at_s)
306	}

308	/// The environment grade: a verdict on the **box**, scored from
309	/// the warmup micro-probe series.
310	///
311	/// - The run grade's signals carry the workload's character — a
312	///   blocking round-trip is genuinely less steady than a spinning
313	///   one, so its letter describes the bench as much as the
314	///   machine. The probes touch no bench at all, so this letter is
315	///   the machine alone. That separation is the whole point:
316	///   warmup is the only workload-independent window a run has.
317	/// - Four signals, worst wins, same arithmetic as [`RunGrade`],
318	///   scored against [`env_thresholds`].
319	/// - Signal choice against the run grade's four:
320	///   - `interference` and `drift` and `step` — the same
321	///     questions, same definitions, different population.
322	///   - `spread` — **new here.** How wide a probe's bulk sits
323	///     above its own floor. There is no run-side analog worth
324	///     having: a bench's spread is mostly its workload (park /
325	///     unpark bimodality is a fact about `mpsc`, not the box),
326	///     while a timer pair has no character of its own, so its
327	///     width is the machine's.
328	///   - `bursts` — **dropped.** With [`crate::harness::ENV_PROBES`]
329	///     probes the hot-fraction is granular to 1/16, and the
330	///     contamination it would count is already counted by
331	///     `interference` at group resolution.
332	/// - **What the probe cannot see.** It measures the box only
333	///   while the measuring thread is running, so time the thread
334	///   spends descheduled is largely invisible: a ~256 µs probe
335	///   usually fits inside one scheduling quantum and completes
336	///   without being preempted at all. Measured on the 3900X,
337	///   sharing the pinned core with one spinner moved
338	///   `interference` from 0.01% to 0.04% and with three spinners
339	///   it read 0.01% — while `spread` (0.31% to 2.02%) and
340	///   `drift`/`step` (A to D) responded properly. So this grade
341	///   detects frequency and state movement well and preemption
342	///   poorly; `interference` catches only the rare large
343	///   intrusion that lands inside a probe.
344	/// - This is the grade that could earn warnings later: an F here
345	///   is a statement about the machine, which is actionable in a
346	///   way that an F on a blocking bench is not. Nothing warns yet.
347	#[derive(Debug)]
348	pub struct EnvGrade {
349	    /// Median over probes of each probe's spread: its upper
350	    /// quantile over its floor, relative.
351	    pub spread_frac: f64,
352	    /// Individual timer pairs above their probe's over-floor
353	    /// cut, as a fraction of all pairs in the series.
354	    pub interference_frac: f64,
355	    /// Floor movement from the first quarter of the probe series
356	    /// to the last, relative.
357	    pub drift_frac: f64,
358	    /// The largest floor shift any split of the series divides,
359	    /// relative.
360	    pub step_frac: f64,
361	    /// Where that split fell — seconds from warmup start.
362	    pub step_at_s: f64,
363	    /// Overall letter, worst signal wins: A, B, C, D, or F.
364	    pub letter: char,
365	}
366	
367	impl EnvGrade {
368	    /// Grade the environment from the warmup probe series; `None`
369	    /// when warmup produced no probes.
370	    pub fn from_probes(probes: &[ProbeSummary]) -> Option<Self> {
371	        if probes.is_empty() {
372	            return None;
373	        }
374	
375	        let spreads: Vec<f64> = probes
376	            .iter()
377	            .map(|p| {
378	                if p.floor_q_ps == 0 {
379	                    0.0
380	                } else {
381	                    (p.spread_q_ps as f64 - p.floor_q_ps as f64) / p.floor_q_ps as f64
382	                }
383	            })
384	            .collect();
385	        let spread_frac = median(&spreads).unwrap_or(0.0); // OK: `probes` is non-empty
386	
387	        let total: u64 = probes.iter().map(|p| p.pairs).sum();
388	        let over: u64 = probes.iter().map(|p| p.over_pairs).sum();
389	        let interference_frac = if total == 0 {
390	            0.0
391	        } else {
392	            over as f64 / total as f64
393	        };
394	
395	        let floors: Vec<f64> = probes.iter().map(|p| p.floor_q_ps as f64).collect();
396	        let n = floors.len();
397	        let quarter = (n / 4).max(1);
398	        let drift_frac = split_change(&floors[..quarter], &floors[n - quarter..]);
399	
400	        let times: Vec<f64> = probes.iter().map(|p| p.t_start_s).collect();
401	        let (step_frac, step_at_s) = best_split(&floors, &times);
402	
403	        let mut grade = Self {
404	            spread_frac,
405	            interference_frac,
406	            drift_frac,
407	            step_frac,
408	            step_at_s,
409	            letter: 'A',
410	        };
411	        grade.letter = score_letter(grade.scores().into_iter().fold(0, u8::max));
412	        Some(grade)
413	    }
414	
415	    /// Per-signal scores in print order: spread, interference,
416	    /// drift, step — each the count of its [`env_thresholds`]
417	    /// cutoffs crossed, composite is the worst.
418	    fn scores(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
419	        [
420	            score(self.spread_frac, env_thresholds::SPREAD),
421	            score(self.interference_frac, env_thresholds::INTERFERENCE),
422	            score(self.drift_frac, env_thresholds::DRIFT),
423	            score(self.step_frac, env_thresholds::STEP),
424	        ]
425	    }
426	
427	    /// Letters for the gauge line's printed signals, in print
428	    /// order — all four composite inputs, so the worst letter on
429	    /// the line *is* the composite.
430	    pub fn signal_letters(&self) -> [char; 4] {
431	        self.scores().map(score_letter)
432	    }
433	}

435	/// Relative change between two runs of floors, each summarized by
436	/// its median: `|median(b) - median(a)| / median(a)`. Zero when
437	/// either side is empty or the earlier median is not positive.
438	fn split_change(a: &[f64], b: &[f64]) -> f64 {
439	    match (median(a), median(b)) {
440	        (Some(early), Some(late)) if early > 0.0 => (late - early).abs() / early,
441	        _ => 0.0,
442	    }
443	}
444	
445	/// Median of a slice, `None` when empty. Copies to sort — the
446	/// slices are batch counts, not sample counts.
447	fn median(v: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> {
448	    if v.is_empty() {
449	        return None;
450	    }
451	    let mut s = v.to_vec();
452	    s.sort_by(f64::total_cmp);
453	    Some(s[s.len() / 2])
454	}

535	        // split point, and the balance term lands it between them.
536	    }
537	
538	    #[test]
539	    fn transient_batch_is_not_a_transition() {
540	        // One hot batch in twenty: a burst, not a state change —
541	        // the medians on both sides of every split are unmoved.
542	        // (The adjacent-pair detector this replaced read 20%.)
543	        let g =
544	            RunGrade::from_batches(&run_of(&[(10, 1000), (1, 1200), (9, 1000)])).expect("graded");
545	        assert_eq!(g.drift_frac, 0.0);
546	        assert_eq!(g.step_frac, 0.0);
547	        assert_eq!(g.letter, 'A');
548	    }
549	
550	    #[test]
551	    fn census_counts_drive_interference() {
552	        let mut batches = steady(2, 1000, 1010.0, 0);
553	        batches[0].over_floor = 100;
554	        let g = RunGrade::from_batches(&batches).expect("graded");
555	        assert!((g.interference_frac - 0.05).abs() < 1e-9);
556	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters()[0], 'B');
557	    }
558	
559	    #[test]
560	    fn hot_batches_drive_bursts() {
561	        // Three of ten means sit > 5% above the median batch.
562	        let mut batches = steady(10, 1000, 1000.0, 0);
563	        for b in batches.iter_mut().take(3) {
564	            b.mean_ps = 1200.0;
565	        }
566	        let g = RunGrade::from_batches(&batches).expect("graded");
567	        assert!((g.burst_frac - 0.3).abs() < 1e-9);
568	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters()[1], 'B');
569	    }
570	
571	    /// One probe with the given floor / upper quantile / census
572	    /// count, stamped at `at` seconds.
573	    fn probe_at(at: f64, floor_ps: u64, spread_q_ps: u64, over_pairs: u64) -> ProbeSummary {
574	        ProbeSummary {
575	            t_start_s: at,
576	            groups: 128,
577	            floor_q_ps: floor_ps,
578	            spread_q_ps,
579	            mean_ps: floor_ps as f64 + 10.0,
580	            pairs: 8192,
581	            over_pairs,
582	        }
583	    }
584	
585	    /// A series of `n` identical probes, one every millisecond.
586	    fn probes(n: usize, floor_ps: u64, spread_q_ps: u64, over_pairs: u64) -> Vec<ProbeSummary> {
587	        (0..n)
588	            .map(|i| probe_at(i as f64 * 0.001, floor_ps, spread_q_ps, over_pairs))
589	            .collect()
590	    }

592	    #[test]
593	    fn warmup_with_no_probes_has_no_grade() {
594	        assert!(EnvGrade::from_probes(&[]).is_none());
595	    }
596	
597	    #[test]
598	    fn quiet_box_grades_a() {
599	        // 25.0 ns floor, 25.2 ns p90: 0.8% spread, no census hits.
600	        let g = EnvGrade::from_probes(&probes(16, 25_000, 25_200, 0)).expect("graded");
601	        assert_eq!(g.letter, 'A');
602	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters(), ['A', 'A', 'A', 'A']);
603	    }
604	
605	    #[test]
606	    fn wide_probes_drive_spread() {
607	        // p90 sits 12% over the floor — past the C cutoff (0.10).
608	        let g = EnvGrade::from_probes(&probes(16, 25_000, 28_000, 0)).expect("graded");
609	        assert!((g.spread_frac - 0.12).abs() < 1e-9);
610	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters()[0], 'D');
611	        assert_eq!(g.letter, 'D');
612	    }
613	
614	    #[test]
615	    fn census_counts_drive_env_interference() {
616	        let mut ps = probes(16, 25_000, 25_200, 0);
617	        // 1,024 of 131,072 pairs over the cut: 0.78%, past the
618	        // 0.005 cutoff and short of 0.02.
619	        ps[0].over_pairs = 1_024;
620	        let g = EnvGrade::from_probes(&ps).expect("graded");
621	        assert!((g.interference_frac - 0.0078125).abs() < 1e-9);
622	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters()[1], 'C');
623	    }
624	
625	    #[test]
626	    fn a_ramping_box_lights_drift_and_step() {
627	        // The frequency ramp this grade exists to catch: the
628	        // floor settles 20% lower halfway through warmup.
629	        let mut ps = probes(16, 30_000, 30_200, 0);
630	        for (i, p) in ps.iter_mut().enumerate().skip(8) {
631	            p.floor_q_ps = 24_000;
632	            p.spread_q_ps = 24_160;
633	            p.t_start_s = i as f64 * 0.001;
634	        }
635	        let g = EnvGrade::from_probes(&ps).expect("graded");
636	        assert!((g.drift_frac - 0.2).abs() < 1e-9);
637	        assert!((g.step_frac - 0.2).abs() < 1e-9);
638	        assert!((g.step_at_s - 0.008).abs() < 1e-9);
639	        assert_eq!(g.signal_letters(), ['A', 'A', 'F', 'F']);
640	    }

642	    #[test]
643	    fn one_disturbed_probe_is_not_a_transition() {
644	        // A single slow probe among sixteen: the medians on both
645	        // sides of every split are unmoved.
646	        let mut ps = probes(16, 25_000, 25_200, 0);
647	        ps[9].floor_q_ps = 40_000;
648	        let g = EnvGrade::from_probes(&ps).expect("graded");
649	        assert_eq!(g.drift_frac, 0.0);
650	        assert_eq!(g.step_frac, 0.0);
651	        assert_eq!(g.letter, 'A');
652	    }
653	
654	    #[test]
655	    fn a_broad_bench_is_not_bursty() {
656	        // Batch means scattered ±4% around the median: spread,
657	        // not bursts. Against the *quietest* batch this read 100%.
658	        let mut batches = steady(10, 1000, 1000.0, 0);
659	        for (i, b) in batches.iter_mut().enumerate() {
660	            b.mean_ps = if i % 2 == 0 { 1000.0 } else { 1040.0 };
661	        }
662	        let g = RunGrade::from_batches(&batches).expect("graded");
663	        assert_eq!(g.burst_frac, 0.0);
664	    }

1	//! Generic bench driver: the [`Bench`] trait, adaptive outer/inner
2	//! loop sizing, and the band-histogram report.
3	
4	use std::hint::black_box;
5	
6	use hdrhistogram::Histogram;
7	
8	use crate::bands::{self, BandLabels};
9	use crate::dither::Dither;
10	
11	const WARMUP: u64 = 10_000;
12	const ESTIMATE_STEPS: u64 = 1_000;
13	const ESTIMATE_SAMPLES: usize = 5;
14	const FRAMING_DOMINATION_RATIO: f64 = 10.0;
15	const MAX_INNER: u64 = 1_000;
16	
17	/// Timer pairs per *timed group* inside a micro-probe.
18	///
19	/// - The probe's unit of measurement is a group, not a single
20	///   pair: one `Instant` pair brackets [`PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`]
21	///   pairs and the total is divided down to a per-pair value.
22	/// - **Why group at all:** the timer reads integer nanoseconds,
23	///   so a single ~25 ns pair is quantized to ~4% — coarser than
24	///   the frequency-ramp movement the environment grade exists to
25	///   see (~9% on the 3900X). A 64-pair group totals ~1.6 µs, so
26	///   the same 1 ns quantum is ~0.06% of the value, and the
27	///   per-pair figure lands on a ~15 ps lattice.
28	/// - Grouping costs the *census* its sensitivity, so the census
29	///   is counted per pair instead — see [`Prober::probe`].
30	const PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS: usize = 64;
31	
32	/// Timed groups per micro-probe — the population its floor and
33	/// spread quantiles are taken over.
34	///
35	/// - 128 groups of [`PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`] is ~8,192 pairs, about
36	///   256 µs. Sized against the batch seam it runs in, which
37	///   already costs 1-2 ms (a `select_nth_unstable` plus 65,536
38	///   histogram records), so a probe adds a fraction of a gap
39	///   that already exists rather than a new one.
40	const PROBE_GROUPS: usize = 128;
41	
42	/// Micro-probes taken during warmup, spread evenly across it —
43	/// the leading stretch of the environment series, and the only
44	/// stretch measured before the bench starts running (see
45	/// [`crate::gauge::EnvGrade`]). The rest of the series is
46	/// sampled at batch seams across the whole run.
47	const WARMUP_PROBES: usize = 16;
48	
49	/// Probes at the *end* of the warmup stretch that the warmup
50	/// grade reads — its trailing window.
51	///
52	/// - Warmup's job is to absorb a ramp, so grading the whole
53	///   stretch would fault a warmup that did exactly that. The
54	///   question worth asking is "did it end settled", which is a
55	///   window at the tail.
56	/// - Eight is the smallest window the split detector can work
57	///   in, needing [`crate::gauge::MIN_SPLIT_BATCHES`] a side.
58	/// - The "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo turns this window into
59	///   the *exit condition* — warm until the trailing window
60	///   grades A — at which point the grade and the stopping rule
61	///   are one computation.
62	const WARMUP_TAIL_PROBES: usize = 8;
63	
64	/// Quantile defining a micro-probe's floor, matching
65	/// [`BATCH_FLOOR_Q`]'s reasoning: the left edge is sparse, a
66	/// tenth of the population is not.
67	const ENV_FLOOR_Q: f64 = 0.10;
68	
69	/// Upper quantile paired with [`ENV_FLOOR_Q`] to measure a
70	/// probe's spread — how wide the bulk of the distribution sits
71	/// above its own floor.
72	const ENV_SPREAD_Q: f64 = 0.90;
73	
74	/// Census threshold for a micro-probe group, the batch census
75	/// rule ([`BATCH_OVER_MULT`]) rebased on the probe's scale: the
76	/// additive term is 5 ns rather than 50, because a per-pair
77	/// value is ~25 ns and a 50 ns floor would never be crossed.
78	const ENV_OVER_ADD_PS: u64 = 5_000;
79	
80	/// Batch buffer capacity in samples — the pipeline's memory
81	/// bound (512 KiB of u64 ps values). Fast benches fill it in
82	/// ~15–40 ms and flush full; slow benches flush earlier on
83	/// [`BATCH_TARGET_SECONDS`].
84	const BATCH_SAMPLES: usize = 65_536;
85	
86	/// Time-based batch flush (seconds): a partial batch flushes
87	/// once it spans this long, so slow benches still get a usable
88	/// time axis (drift/burst localization) from few samples.
89	const BATCH_TARGET_SECONDS: f64 = 0.05;
90	
91	/// Push-count mask between time checks in
92	/// [`BatchPipeline::push`] — one `Instant::now` per 1024
93	/// samples keeps the check cost off the per-sample path.
94	const BATCH_CHECK_MASK: usize = 1023;
95	
96	/// Quantile defining a batch's *robust* floor, the statistic the
97	/// gauge's drift/step signals read.
98	///
99	/// - The raw min is too sparse to grade movement: measured on a
100	///   quiet 3900X at inner=10 (100 ps lattice), adjacent batch
101	///   minima flipped between 22.0 and 23.0 ns — a 4.5% "step" on
102	///   a run with no state change, which alone would have graded
103	///   every quiet run F.
104	/// - The same batches' p10 sat on 23.0 ns run-wide and moved
105	///   only when the machine did. The left edge of the
106	///   distribution is sparse; a tenth of 65,536 samples is not.
107	const BATCH_FLOOR_Q: f64 = 0.10;
108	
109	/// Census threshold: a batch sample is "over floor" above
110	/// `max(BATCH_OVER_MULT x floor, floor + BATCH_OVER_ADD_PS)`,
111	/// applied per batch against the batch's own [`BATCH_FLOOR_Q`]
112	/// floor.
113	///
114	/// - Measured against the raw min instead, the census was
115	///   meaningless on any bench with a low tail: mpsc-2t batches
116	///   whose min landed on a 0.9 µs fast path (against a 6.5 µs
117	///   floor) counted 99.9% of their samples "over floor", and the
118	///   ones whose min landed normally counted 1%.
119	const BATCH_OVER_MULT: f64 = 1.5;
120	
121	/// Additive part of the census threshold (50 ns in ps).
122	const BATCH_OVER_ADD_PS: u64 = 50_000;
123	
124	/// Sleep-separated blocks: random sleep bounds (ms) between
125	/// blocks. Randomized so block boundaries don't phase-lock with
126	/// kernel ticks or workload periodicity; long enough to let the
127	/// scheduler / frequency state re-roll.
128	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MIN: u64 = 1;
129	const BLOCK_SLEEP_MS_MAX: u64 = 10;
130	
131	/// Unrecorded post-wake warm-up per block (seconds). Each wake
132	/// pays a frequency ramp plus a cache refill, which must not leak
133	/// into the block's samples.
134	const BLOCK_WARMUP_SECONDS: f64 = 0.002;
135	
136	/// Histogram value bounds: 1 ps to 60 s at 3 sig figs. Values
137	/// are recorded in **picoseconds** — the timer reads integer ns,
138	/// but dividing a sample by `inner` in ps keeps the true sub-ns
139	/// per-call precision that ns recording truncated (a 4.7 ns call
140	/// no longer rounds to 5). The high bound is a sane-world
141	/// ceiling for one recorded sample, not a technical limit —
142	/// [`record_sample`] clamps above it and [`warn_invalid`] flags
143	/// the run.
144	const HIST_LOW_PS: u64 = 1;
145	const HIST_HIGH_PS: u64 = 60_000_000_000_000;
146	
147	/// Picoseconds per nanosecond: recorded values are ps, display
148	/// is ns.
149	const PS_PER_NS: f64 = 1000.0;
150	
151	/// Label-column width for the two gauge blocks, wide enough for
152	/// the longest label (`env worst case:`) plus a gap. Shared so
153	/// the environment and run rows line up under each other.
154	const GAUGE_LABEL_W: usize = 21;
155	
156	/// `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` minus `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` elapsed divergence
157	/// (seconds) at or above which [`warn_invalid`] reports that the
158	/// system suspended during the run.
159	const SUSPEND_WARN_S: f64 = 1.0;
160	
161	/// A benchmark workload: a named operation that `step()` performs
162	/// in a tight loop for sub-µs latency measurement. Implementors own
163	/// any setup state (channels, spawned threads, counters). `step()`
164	/// returns a value so the caller can `black_box` it against dead-code
165	/// elimination.
166	pub trait Bench {
167	    /// Human-readable name used in the report header.
168	    fn name(&self) -> &str;
169	
170	    /// Run one unit of work. Return any value derived from the work
171	    /// to defeat DCE — the caller black-boxes it.
172	    fn step(&mut self) -> u64;
173	}
174	
175	/// Runtime configuration for one [`run_adaptive`] call.
176	#[derive(Debug)]
177	pub struct RunCfg<'a> {
178	    /// Wall-clock seconds budget for time-based runs. Ignored when
179	    /// `outer_override` is set.
180	    pub target_seconds: f64,
181	    /// Force a fixed outer-loop count, bypassing the time budget.
182	    pub outer_override: Option<u64>,
183	    /// Force a fixed inner-loop count, bypassing the
184	    /// micro-probe-driven auto-sizing.
185	    pub inner_override: Option<u64>,

content.content:
### Two boxes, two failure modes

The thresholds were checked on both machines. The design
constraint they answer to: a quiet release-build box should
essentially never leave A/B, or a false alarm every third run
destroys trust in the warning.

On the **quiet 7600x** (2026-07-28, built and run on the box, not
a copied binary), `iiac-perf all -d 2` graded A on 12 of 16
benches — every single-threaded bench and every spinning one.
Ten back-to-back `min-now -d 1` runs at zero gap graded **A ten
times**, `drift` and `step` both 0.00% on each, `interference`
steady at 0.02–0.03%. That is the same cadence
[qualify_environment.rs](../../tests/qualify_environment.rs) runs, whose
observable is the *calibrate* letter — it read nine A and one B
(`repeat ±0.29 ns`) on the same box in the same session, so the
gauge is at least as clean as the check it will replace.

The exceptions were the **blocking** mpsc round-trips, `mpsc-2t`
and `probe-mpsc-2t`, at `step` F (12–17% floor shift), plus
`ice-ps-2t` and `zcr-mpsc-2t` at C. Pinning to a core pair did
not clear them — six pinned runs still produced three F's —
while `mpsc-2t-spin`, the same round-trip spinning instead of
parking, graded A. We think the blocking path's floor is
genuinely bimodal (a hot handoff versus an actual park/unpark),
which is a property of the bench, not the box.

That pair is what settled the reports-never-warns rule above.
The warnings had asserted "the machine changed state mid-run" —
wrong on exactly these benches, where the movement is the
workload's. Two intermediate versions were tried and discarded
first: deleting the cause outright (which left a reader with a
percentage and nothing to do with it), then hedging the cause and
naming a check. Both still framed the letter as a fault. It
isn't one, and the fix was to stop warning rather than to keep
rewording the warning.

### What the gauge says about the 3900X

content.content:
### What the gauge says about the 3900X

Here the movement *was* the machine: unpinned 2-thread benches
graded D on floor movement and moved to A/C when pinned to a core
pair, with nothing else changed. We think that is placement
instability being reported honestly — an unpinned 2-thread run on
a 3900X mixes core placements, and the floor moves when it does.
The contrast with the 7600x's blocking-mpsc F's, which pinning
did *not* clear, is what makes the two cases distinguishable at
all.

On the same box, min-now runs grade A on some invocations and D
(step ~8.7%, a 22 → 24 ns floor shift) on others, at both 1 s and
3 s budgets. That is the settle anomaly
([qualify_environment.rs](../../tests/qualify_environment.rs)) showing up
in the run rather than in calibration. Chasing which bench the
selftest should read to see that reliably is what exposed the
deeper problem: any answer would have been a workload chosen to
approximate a workload-independent question. The -4 environment
grade answers it directly, from the warmup micro-probe, so the
selftest reads that and needs no bench at all.
The thresholds were left where they are
rather than widened to absorb it: the box really is bistable, and
the dynamic-warmup Todo is the fix.

The three mechanical parts are in and working. Here's what the box says.

**Report line now** (this 3900X, `min-now -d 2`):

```
env warmup:  settled 1.03s, spread 0.30% A, interference 0.01% A, drift 0.00% A, step 0.00% A
env run:     spread 0.37% A, interference 0.01% A, drift 9.92% D, step 9.92% @2.53s D
env worst case:  D
```

What changed: a 1.5 s process warm before the first bench (bench 1's warmup stretch is now ~150 probes at 10 ms instead of 16 at 1 ms; later benches unchanged), the graded window is the last 300 ms of warmup rather than the last 8 probes, and the warmup row leads with settle time.

Two things I had to iterate on, both because settle time disagreed with the letter beside it:

- A suffix-median rule read `settled 0.00s` on stretches whose own `drift` graded F — a minority of moved probes never shifts a median.
- A per-probe rule then read `settled 1.51s` ("never settled") beside `drift 0.00% A` — this box's floor flickers across a 1% band constantly while every median stays put. Settle time now asks the question of an 8-probe window median, the same granularity the step signal uses, and the two agree on all runs I've seen.

**On the warm length.** The 1.5 s absorbs the startup ramp cleanly — warmup grades A with settle landing 0.09–1.03 s. But this box's ~10% relaxation is not a startup ramp: at 1.5 s it lands ~2.5 s in (inside the bench), and at 3.5 s I still got 2 of 4 runs moving, at 4.4 s and 4.6 s — once *inside* the warmup tail. So the 3900X's transition recurs at arbitrary times and no warm length reaches it. That's the known bistability whose fix is the Dynamic startup warmup Todo; 1.5 s is doing the job it was scoped for.

That last point bears on the two open decisions:

1. **Composite.** At 3.5 s I saw a warmup row grade D from a real transition inside the tail. So "a transition inside warmup is warmup working" isn't universally true — it's true of a *ramp*, not of this box's relapses. Dropping warmup from the composite would have hidden that D. My inclination is to keep worst-of-two and treat the time-based window as the actual fix, but it's your call.
2. **Qualify.** Untouched so far, and it still parses (I taught `parse_stretch` to skip the non-letter `settled …` segment). Whether it gains a `settle` column, and whether that column can fail a box, is easier to judge once you've run `qualify-environment` against this — want me to run it?

content.text:
Let me correct the 3900X claim first — I overstated it.

**What the data says about this box.** The floor sits in one of two states, ~22 ns and ~24 ns, and it moves between them at arbitrary times — during warmup, mid-bench, or not at all in a given run. That's a ~9–10% shift in absolute latency. It doesn't make the box useless for microbenchmarking; it constrains what you can conclude from one run:

- Absolute numbers carry ~10% of state noise, so "this operation costs 22.0 ns" is only true of the state it was measured in.
- Same-harness A/B still works, because both sides are exposed to the same bistability — that's what `--blocks` (sleep-separated replicates, CI and LSC) exists for, and what the run grade's letter tells you to look at before trusting a single-run delta.
- What it does mean is that this box will not pass a test whose criterion is "no state transition landed inside a measurement window", because transitions genuinely do. The 7600x, per the earlier notes, is quiet on that same test. So `qualify-environment` is doing its job: it says *this machine needs replication*, not *this machine is worthless*.

**Definition of settle.** Precisely what the code computes:

- The input is the warmup stretch's probe series. Each probe contributes one floor: the p10 of its 128 timed group means, in picoseconds. Nothing from the bench enters — only timer pairs.
- The **settled level** is the median floor of the tail window (the last 300 ms of warmup) — i.e. where the box was when measurement was about to start.
- Each position in the series gets a **window median**: the median of the next 8 probe floors from it (windows anchor at the end rather than shrinking). 8 probes is ~80 ms during the process warm.
- A window is **out of band** when its median differs from the settled level by more than 1% — the same 1% the environment grade's `drift`/`step` use for their A cutoff.
- **Settle time is the timestamp of the probe following the last out-of-band window**, in seconds from warmup start. Zero means the box was already there when we started looking.

So: *how long before the floor entered — and stayed inside — a ±1% band around the level warmup ended at.*

Three things that definition does **not** say, which are easy to read into it:

- It is relative to where *this* warmup ended, not to any correct or maximal speed. A run that warms up into the slow state reports its fast early stretch as "unsettled" — settle time never says which state is the right one.
- It's biased early by up to one window (~80 ms): the first window that reads settled straddles the last of the ramp.
- The `1.51s` readings are an artifact of the current fallback — the last window was still out of band, so it reports the final probe's time. That is "never settled" wearing a number, which is exactly the misreading you're guarding against.

Taking your steer: settle stays out of the verdict, and I'll print `not settled` (`not` in the qualify column) instead of that number.

On `--settle-time` I need one clarification before wiring it, because three different knobs fit the name:

1. **Warm duration** — replaces the hard-coded 1.5 s: `--settle-time 3` warms for 3 s. Simple, but it's a fixed budget, not a convergence rule.
2. **Warm budget with early exit** — warm *until settled*, giving up at `--settle-time`. This is the Dynamic startup warmup Todo's actual mechanism, arriving a rung early. On this box it would burn the whole budget most runs.
3. **The band** — `--settle-time` sets the 1% tolerance instead, changing what counts as settled without changing how long we warm.

Which did you mean? My guess is 1 for this rung, leaving 2 to the Todo that owns it.

1	//! The `qualify-environment` selftest: is this machine fit to
2	//! measure on?
3	//!
4	//! Respawns our own binary `--runs` times at `--gap`, collects
5	//! each run's environment grade, prints the table, and returns a
6	//! verdict. It tests the *machine*, not a workload, so it reads
7	//! the environment stretches rather than the run grade — see
8	//! [`crate::gauge::EnvGrade`].
9	//!
10	//! - **Why respawn** rather than loop in-process: a fresh process
11	//!   per run is what terminal use looks like, and in-process
12	//!   repeats would share warmed state — the very thing under
13	//!   test.
14	//! - **Why `min-now`** as the child workload: the box is the
15	//!   subject, so the leanest available bench is right. It also
16	//!   measures nearly what the probe measures, which keeps the run
17	//!   grade and the environment grade commensurable.
18	//! - **The verdict** is grades, not values: median environment
19	//!   grade at B or better, and no run whose `drift` or `step`
20	//!   reached D/F in either stretch. Those two are the transition
21	//!   detectors, so a D/F there is a state change landing inside a
22	//!   measurement window — the anomaly this test exists to catch.
23	//!   Wobble on `spread` or `interference` is ambient
24	//!   contamination and does not fail the run.
25	
26	use std::process::Command;
27	use std::time::Duration;
28	
29	use crate::gauge::Settle;
30	
31	/// Child bench: the leanest registered workload, so the table
32	/// reflects the box rather than a workload's character.
33	const CHILD_BENCH: &str = "min-now";
34	
35	/// Knobs for one selftest, from the CLI.
36	pub struct QualifyCfg {
37	    /// Child runs to spawn.
38	    pub runs: u64,
39	    /// Sleep before each child. Zero sustains the duty cycle that
40	    /// provokes a transition; a nonzero gap probes a quieter one.
41	    pub gap_s: f64,
42	    /// Wall-clock seconds per child run.
43	    pub duration_s: f64,
44	    /// `--pin` spec to pass through, if any.
45	    pub pin: Option<String>,
46	    /// Print the table and skip the verdict.
47	    pub print_only: bool,
48	    /// `--settle-time` to pass each child, when the parent was
49	    /// given one. Absent leaves each child on its own default, so
50	    /// the table reflects what a plain run of this binary does.
51	    pub settle_time: Option<f64>,
52	}
53	
54	/// One environment stretch parsed from a child's report: its
55	/// composite letter and the per-signal blob behind it.
56	struct Stretch {
57	    letter: char,
58	    signals: String,
59	}
60	
61	/// A warmup row's leading settle segment — `settled 0.84s` or
62	/// `not settled`; `None` on any row that carries neither (the run
63	/// stretch, or a child too old to print one).
64	fn parse_settle(line: &str) -> Option<Settle> {
65	    line.split(", ").find_map(|s| match s.trim() {
66	        "not settled" => Some(Settle::Never),
67	        seg => seg
68	            .strip_prefix("settled ")
69	            .and_then(|v| v.trim_end_matches('s').parse().ok())
70	            .map(Settle::At),
71	    })
72	}
73	
74	impl Stretch {
75	    /// Letter of one named signal — each `, `-separated segment
76	    /// ends with its own letter.
77	    fn signal_letter(&self, name: &str) -> Option<char> {
78	        self.signals
79	            .split(", ")
80	            .find(|s| s.trim().starts_with(name))
81	            .and_then(|s| s.trim().chars().last())
82	    }
83	
84	    /// True when a transition detector reached D/F here.
85	    fn transition_degraded(&self) -> bool {
86	        ["drift", "step"]
87	            .into_iter()
88	            .any(|s| self.signal_letter(s).is_some_and(|l| l == 'D' || l == 'F'))
89	    }
90	}
91	
92	/// One child run's parsed result.
93	struct QualifyRun {
94	    warmup: Option<Stretch>,
95	    during: Option<Stretch>,
96	    /// Environment composite — the worse of the two stretches, as
97	    /// the child computed it.
98	    worst: char,
99	    /// The run's mean, for the value column: the number that makes
100	    /// a two-state box visible at a glance.
101	    mean: String,
102	    /// How long the child's warmup took to settle — how much
103	    /// warming this box needs before it is worth measuring on,
104	    /// read across respawns. Reported, not judged: the verdict
105	    /// stays grades, because a box still moving at the end of
106	    /// warmup already shows up as a drift/step D/F on the warmup
107	    /// stretch.
108	    settle: Option<Settle>,
109	}
110	
111	impl QualifyRun {
112	    /// True when either stretch shows a transition at D/F.
113	    fn transition_degraded(&self) -> bool {
114	        [self.warmup.as_ref(), self.during.as_ref()]
115	            .into_iter()
116	            .flatten()
117	            .any(Stretch::transition_degraded)
118	    }
119	
120	    /// Per-stretch letters for the table, `-` where a stretch is
121	    /// absent (`--no-env-probe` leaves no run stretch).
122	    fn letters(&self) -> (char, char) {
123	        (
124	            self.warmup.as_ref().map_or('-', |s| s.letter),
125	            self.during.as_ref().map_or('-', |s| s.letter),
126	        )
127	    }
128	}
129	
130	/// Letter -> ordinal score, A best. Unknown letters score worst,
131	/// so a parse miss can never flatter a run.
132	fn score(letter: char) -> i64 {
133	    match letter {
134	        'A' => 5,
135	        'B' => 4,
136	        'C' => 3,
137	        'D' => 2,
138	        _ => 1,
139	    }
140	}
141	
142	/// Inverse of [`score`], for reporting a median back as a letter.
143	fn letter_for(score: i64) -> char {
144	    match score {
145	        5 => 'A',
146	        4 => 'B',
147	        3 => 'C',
148	        2 => 'D',
149	        _ => 'F',
150	    }
151	}
152	
153	/// Parse one `env <name>:` row into a [`Stretch`]: the composite
154	/// is carried separately, so this keeps the signal blob and the
155	/// row's own worst letter.
156	fn parse_stretch(line: &str) -> Stretch {
157	    // Every signal segment ends with its letter; the row's worst

7	//!   series ([`ProbeSummary`]): how steady was the machine,
8	//!   measured on the apparatus alone before any workload entered
9	//!   the numbers.
10	//!
11	//! They share their arithmetic (signals scored against ascending
12	//! cutoffs, worst signal wins, every signal printing its own
13	//! letter) and deliberately not their thresholds or their signal
14	//! sets. A bench that reads F on the run grade and A on the
15	//! environment grade is a true and useful statement: the workload
16	//! is bursty on a quiet machine.
17	//!
18	//! Every signal is computed from the batches the run itself
19	//! produced, so the letter describes the data being reported
20	//! rather than a window measured beforehand.
21	//!
22	//! - Four signals, each scored against its own ascending cutoffs
23	//!   (A..F); the composite letter is the worst of them, and each
24	//!   signal prints its own letter beside its value so the
25	//!   composite always names its cause. See
26	//!   [`RunGrade::scores`] for the arithmetic and
27	//!   [`thresholds`] for the cutoffs.
28	//! - Four, where the startup calibration grade this replaced had
29	//!   six. Two of those six graded how well a *fit* held (a
30	//!   ladder point's residual against the Theil-Sen line, and the
31	//!   loop-only slope against the dithered two-point fit), and a
32	//!   bench run fits nothing: no line for a point to sit off, no
33	//!   second estimator to cross-check. Inventing a fit just to
34	//!   grade it would have been the wrong direction. The full
35	//!   mapping is recorded in
36	//!   notes/chores/chores-05.md#six-calibration-signals-four-run-signals.

38	//!   measurement: `drift` asks whether the run ended where it
39	//!   began, `step` looks for a shift anywhere inside it and says
40	//!   when. A run that shifts and shifts back is invisible to the
41	//!   first and obvious to the second.

45	//!   batches whose mean sits above the typical one (whether that
46	//!   interference was localized in time or spread evenly).

50	//! on a quiet 7600x the blocking mpsc round-trips read step F

53	//! the bench, not the box. An F there is a true description of
54	//! what was measured, not a fault to raise, and the report's job
55	//! is a faithful histogram rather than a verdict. The verdict on
56	//! the box is a separate grade measured during warmup, where the
57	//! workload's character hasn't entered the numbers yet.

99	pub mod env_thresholds {
100	    /// Probe spread: the p90-over-floor width of a typical probe.
101	    pub const SPREAD: [f64; 4] = [0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25];
102	    /// Census rate across the probe series: individual timer
103	    /// pairs above their probe's over-floor cut, as a fraction of
104	    /// all pairs. Counted per pair rather than per timed group

What it runs is, in metrology terms, a repeatability study of the
apparatus plus the machine — which is why the grading module is
called `gauge`.

```

  1     A       A        A       22.2 ns
  2     D       A        D       22.2 ns
  3     A       C        C       22.5 ns

  median environment grade: A
  transition-degraded (drift or step at D/F): 1 of 3

  verdict: NOT QUALIFIED
    a state transition landed inside a measurement window
```

It reads the environment grade rather than the run grade,
because the subject is the box: `warmup` is its settling
behaviour across respawns, `env-run` whether it then held. The
verdict is grades, not values — median at B or better, and no
run whose `drift` or `step` reached D/F, those two being the
transition detectors. `spread` and `interference` wobble is
ambient contamination and does not fail a run. The `mean` column
is informational, and it is where a two-state machine shows
itself at a glance.

Each child runs `min-now` for `-d` seconds (default 1): the box
is the subject, so the leanest bench is the right one. `--pin`
passes through to the children, and `--print-only` prints the

  replication count: more blocks → tighter CI but shorter
  blocks. Interpretation: an honest *within-invocation* error
  bar; treat it as a lower bound on cross-invocation
  confidence and pin the bench (`--pin`) — unpinned,
  per-process thread placement dominates and blocks can't see

  [validation](notes/design.md#block-validation-results-0210-4-r5-7600x)

  probing perturbs a spinning multi-threaded bench by ~0.9%

Every report ends with two grades (A–F), each computed from its
own data: `env` for the **box**, `run` for *that run*. Each
signal prints its own letter beside its value, and each
composite prints under its signals on its own line:

```
  env warmup:          spread 0.47% A, interference 0.00% A, drift 0.00% A, step 0.00% A
  env run:             spread 0.48% A, interference 0.00% A, drift 11.05% F, step 11.05% @1.06s F
  env worst case:      F
  run:                 interference 0.04% A, bursts 37% B, drift 10.49% F, step 10.49% @1.04s F
  run worst case:      F
```

The `env` rows are two stretches of one probe series, scored
separately: `warmup` is the trailing window of the probes taken
before the bench ran ("did the box end settled"), `run` the
probes taken alongside it ("did it stay settled"). The composite
is the worse of the two — starting a measurement on a box that
hadn't settled is a real problem — and the split is there so you
can see which stretch earned the letter. They are graded apart
rather than as one series because absorbing a ramp is exactly
what warmup is *for*: blended, the boundary between a cold
warmup and a hot run reads as a large step that nothing actually
did wrong.

They answer different questions, and reading them together says
more than either alone. `run` describes the numbers above it —
and a run's steadiness is largely its workload's character, so a
blocking round-trip reads worse than a spinning one, correctly.
`env` describes the machine: it comes from micro-probes that time
timer pairs and never touch the bench, so no workload character
enters it. An `env` A beside a `run` D means a bursty workload on
a quiet box. The same letter in both, at the same instant, means
the box moved and took the bench with it, as in the example
above: `min-now` on a 7600x, where the environment reports an
11.05% step at 1.06 s and the run reports a 10.49% step at
1.04 s. Same magnitude, same instant, from two series that share
a time axis but not an instrument. Neither grade could make that
call alone.

The probes run through warmup and then in the seam at every batch
boundary, so the series covers the whole run on the same time
axis as the batches. `--no-env-probe` limits them to warmup (so
only the `env warmup` row appears),
which costs the grade its span; it exists because seam probing
perturbs a spinning multi-threaded bench by ~0.9% (measured on
`zcr-with-2t`), a bias that is common-mode in an A/B between two
benches but not in an absolute number.

The `env` signals differ slightly from the run's: `spread` (how
wide a probe's bulk sits above its own floor) replaces `bursts`,

separately: `warmup` is the trailing window of the probes taken
before the bench ran ("did the box end settled"), `run` the
probes taken alongside it ("did it stay settled"). The composite

hadn't settled is a real problem — and the split is there so you
can see which stretch earned the letter. They are graded apart
rather than as one series because absorbing a ramp is exactly

Flags (also visible via `-h` / `--help`):
- `-d`, `--duration SECONDS` — target wall-clock seconds per bench
  (default `5.0`); the outer loop runs until this time is reached
  (inner auto-sizes). See chores `0.3.1-dev1` for the empirical
  recording captures (values are recorded internally in ps and
  displayed in ns); `0` restores integer ns; `3` is the
  recording floor — more digits would be artifacts.
- `--blocks N` — N (2–1000) is the **number of measurement
  blocks** the run's budget is divided into: `--blocks 10`
  with `-d 10` measures 10 blocks of ~1 s each (total measured
  time still 10 s; with `-o` the sample count is divided
  instead). Between blocks the harness sleeps a random 1–10 ms
  (fixed internal range — it re-rolls scheduler/frequency
  state) and warms up unrecorded (~2 ms); neither is counted
  in the budget. The report gains three lines — `mean blocks`
  (mean of the N block means), `CI95` (95% **c**onfidence
  **i**nterval half-width on it), and `LSC` (**l**east
  **s**ignificant **c**hange vs an equal-N run) — and the
  header records `blocks=N`. N is also the statistical
  absolute number. See [The two grades](#the-two-grades).

  default the process re-execs itself under
  `systemd-inhibit --what=sleep` so an idle-suspend can't poison a
  long measurement (a mid-sample suspend inflates that sample by
  the whole sleep gap; see the `WARNING` lines below). Where
  `systemd-inhibit` is unavailable — absent, or the lock is
  denied (e.g. a headless ssh session with no polkit
  interactive auth) — the run continues uninhibited and the
  banner's `sleep inhibit` line says so. Pass this flag to
  keep the process image untouched (strace/gdb/perf wrappers), to
  let the machine sleep on purpose, or to test the
  suspend-detection path — a sleep inhibitor also blocks manual
  `systemctl suspend`.
- `-t`, `--ticks` — show `TProbe` results in raw hardware tick
  counts (`tk`; x86_64 TSC, aarch64 `CNTVCT_EL0`) instead of
  converting to nanoseconds. Only affects `TProbe`-based benches

The `env warmup:` row leads with how long the box took to settle
— `settled 0.86s`, or `not settled` when it was still moving
when warmup ended. It exists because warmup now *absorbs* the
box coming up to speed rather than being graded on it: the first
run of a process spends `--settle-time` seconds (default 1.5)
stepping the bench before recording anything, so the letter
answers "was it settled when measurement started" and this
answers "how long did that take".

The warm is per **process**, not per bench: the boost it wins is
machine state, so every later bench in the same process inherits
it. Without it the first bench of a process reports a cold
machine's numbers — measured at ~8.6% slow on a 7600x, a wrong
histogram rather than merely a wrong letter — while benches 2..N
read correctly. Cost is ~2% of an `all -d 5` sweep.

Settle time is *when the floor entered, and stayed inside, ±1% of
the level warmup ended at*. Precisely: each probe's floor is its
p10 group cost; the settled level is the median floor over the
300 ms tail window; a running 8-probe median (a quarter of the
series when it is shorter than that, matching what `drift`
compares) has to sit inside the band; and the reported time is
the probe after the last one that didn't. Two things it does not
say — it is measured against where *this* warmup ended, not any
absolute best speed, so it never says which state was the right
one; and it is biased early by up to one window, since the first
window that reads settled straddles the last of the ramp.

`--settle-time 0` skips the warm, which is how you measure what
it is worth on a given box. A box that reads `not settled` at
the default wants more, though that is not always curable: on a
3900X the floor is bistable and moves at arbitrary times, so a
3.5 s warm still left runs moving mid-bench. Replication
(`--blocks`) is the answer there, not a longer warm.

Defaults and named pin profiles can live in a TOML config file, so
common invocations don't repeat flags. Precedence, lowest to
highest:

- **built-in defaults** — `duration=5.0`, `band_labels=both`,
  `decimals=1`;
- **XDG file** — `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/iiac-perf/config.toml`, or
  `$HOME/.config/iiac-perf/config.toml` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is
  unset; the per-user home for defaults and profiles;
- **project-local file** — `iiac-perf.toml` in the current
  directory (no upward walk); overrides the XDG file field by
  field, profiles merging by key;
- **CLI flags** — always win.

The startup banner's `config` line names the files that were
loaded (or `none (built-in defaults)`). A present-but-malformed
file is a hard error rather than a silent fallback, so a typo
surfaces. Every key is optional;
[`iiac-perf.toml.example`](iiac-perf.toml.example) is a ready-to-copy
sample documenting each key and its possible values:

```toml
duration     = 10.0     # default -d seconds
band_labels  = "zpn"    # zpn | frac | both
decimals     = 2        # 0-3

[profiles]              # named --pin core specs
smt = "0,12"           # SMT siblings of one physical core (contention)
ccx = "0,1"            # independent cores, same CCX (best channel latency)
ccd = "0,6"            # cross-CCD
```

Each bench prints a band-based histogram in nanoseconds. Each row
is one band, labeled by its **upper boundary**, the lower boundary
being the previous printed row. Bands are **right-closed**
`(lower, upper]` (like `pandas.cut`): a sample whose rank lands
exactly on a boundary counts in the band that boundary *caps*, so a
lone median sample reads `p50`, matching the upper-boundary label
and the CDF sense of a percentile. Labels are deciles in the body
(`p10` … `p90`) and **nines/zeros** notation in both tails, where

band_labels  = "zpn"    # zpn | frac | both
decimals     = 2        # 0-3

[profiles]              # named --pin core specs
smt = "0,12"           # SMT siblings of one physical core (contention)
ccx = "0,1"            # independent cores, same CCX (best channel latency)
ccd = "0,6"            # cross-CCD
```

Each bench prints a band-based histogram in nanoseconds. Each row
is one band, labeled by its **upper boundary**, the lower boundary
being the previous printed row. Bands are **right-closed**
`(lower, upper]` (like `pandas.cut`): a sample whose rank lands
exactly on a boundary counts in the band that boundary *caps*, so a
lone median sample reads `p50`, matching the upper-boundary label
and the CDF sense of a percentile. Labels are deciles in the body
(`p10` … `p90`) and **nines/zeros** notation in both tails, where
`nK`/`zK`

#                                            iiac-perf/config.toml if
#                                            XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset
#   ./iiac-perf.toml                         project-local, current
#                                            directory only (no
#                                            upward walk)
#
# Precedence, lowest to highest:
#   built-in defaults < XDG file < project-local file < CLI flags

# shown here. A present-but-malformed file is a hard error (a typo
# surfaces rather than silently reverting to defaults). The startup

### Settle time is not a grade

Warmup that deliberately spans the box coming up to speed
stops *reporting* that it did: the tail window sits after the
ramp, so the letter goes back to A and the run reads as though
nothing happened. Settle time is what replaces the letter — how
long the box took to reach the state it then measured in.

The definition, in one sentence: when the floor entered, and
stayed inside, ±1% of the level warmup ended at. The mechanics
matter mostly where they were got wrong twice, both times by
disagreeing with the letter printed beside them:

- A **suffix-median** rule read `settled 0.00s` on stretches
  whose own `drift` graded F. A minority of moved probes never
  shifts a median, so the rule reported a box that had visibly
  moved as having never left.
- A **per-probe** rule then read "never settled" beside
  `drift 0.00% A` on the 3900X, whose floor flickers across a
  1% band constantly while every median the grade takes stays
  put.

What settles it is asking the question of the same statistic
the grade uses: a running window median, 8 probes (the step
detector's minimum span) or a quarter of the series when it is
shorter — a quarter being what `drift` compares. On the 16-probe
stretch of a non-first bench, an 8-probe window is half the
series and swallowed an excursion `drift` graded F, which is
what forced the quarter clamp.

Two things the number does not say, both easy to read into it:
it is measured against where *this* warmup ended, so it never
says which state was the right one; and it is biased early by up
to one window, since the first window that reads settled
straddles the last of the ramp.

It is **reported, never judged**. A box still moving when warmup
ends already shows up as a `drift`/`step` D/F on the warmup
stretch, so a settle threshold in the `qualify-environment`
verdict would restate an existing criterion. What the column
adds is the *size* — how much `--settle-time` this box wants —
which is the input the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo turns into
a stopping rule.

We think the reason a warm cannot be a fixed constant is that
the number is per-box: measured 2026-07-30 on the 3900X, the
default 1.5 s absorbs the startup ramp (warmup grades A, settle
landing 0.09–1.36 s across runs), but the box's ~10% bistable
shift then recurs mid-bench. Raising the warm to 3.5 s did not
help — 2 of 4 runs still moved, at 4.4 s and 4.6 s, one of them
inside the warmup tail. That is what kept the composite at
worst-of-two: the plan had the warmup stretch stop counting
because "a transition inside warmup is warmup working", which is
true of a ramp and false of a relapse.

content.text:
Your table shows something the 1.5 s runs hid. Compare medians: at `--settle-time 1.5` settle landed 0.6–1.4 s; at 5 it lands 3.5–5.0 s. Settle time is tracking the *budget*, not the box.

That's inherent to the statistic as defined. Settle is "the probe after the last excursion", and the settled level is the tail window's median — so on a box that keeps flickering, the last excursion is always near the end, whatever the end is. It's an honest reading of "still moving", but it's wearing a number that looks like a property of the machine. The `5.01s` on run 8 versus `not` on runs 4/7/9 is one probe's difference in where the last excursion fell.

Cheap fix, and I'd do it regardless of the bigger question: require a minimum settled tail — if the last excursion is within ~300 ms of the budget's end, report `not settled` rather than a time. Then "settled at T" means the box actually held that state for a while, and the number stops being a budget echo.

**On dropping the bench.** Yes, I think you're right, and the reason is stronger than convenience: the probe already never touches the bench. `min-now` is in the child only to give the warm something to do and to produce a report to parse. Everything the table shows — the letters, the signals, the settle time — comes from the probe series. The `mean` column is the one exception, and the probe's own floor would serve that better, since it's the quantity the grade is actually computed from rather than a second measurement of nearly the same thing.

What it buys: qualification stops depending on a bench's character, the parent stops parsing a full bench report out of prose (the fragility I flagged), and a box with no interesting bench to run still qualifies. What it costs: the warm's character changes — a probe-driven warm is light, and on hardware where a heavy workload drives a different clock/power state (AVX offsets, say) a light warm would qualify the box for the wrong kind of work. On this box that's moot, since `min-now` *is* essentially the probe.

Two sub-questions I'd separate from it:

- **Respawn or loop?** The stated reason for respawning was that in-process repeats share warmed state. That's weaker than it reads: the P-state is the machine's, not the process's — what re-rolls it is the gap and the duty cycle, not the fork. A bench-free qualifier could just loop in-process with gaps, which would also make the results structured data instead of parsed text.
- **"During startup"** — if you mean every run qualifying its box at startup, I'd say no. Each run already reports its own environment grade; qualification needs repeats across time, which is seconds, and a run shouldn't pay that. If you mean the qualifier does its own startup warm rather than borrowing a bench's, that's just the change above.

Scope-wise: this rung is done and the current selftest works, so I'd not fold it into `-8`. It's a rung or a small cycle of its own, and it overlaps the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo (which owns the convergence rule) and the columns Todo (which reformats the table it prints).

*The plain version:* the "settled at 4.63s" numbers aren't telling you how long your machine takes to warm up — they're mostly telling you how long you asked it to warm up, because your machine never really stops moving. I'd make it say "not settled" in those cases. And yes, the environment test doesn't need a benchmark at all: it measures the clock, not the benchmark, so running one is scaffolding we can remove — but as a separate piece of work, not bolted onto this one.

content.text: Implementing the cheap fix — "settled" now requires the state to have held through the graded tail window, which needs no new constant:

content.content:
438	/// - One percent, the same number as [`env_thresholds::DRIFT`]'s
439	///   A cutoff: "settled" means the movement left is movement the
440	///   environment grade would have called A.
441	pub const SETTLE_TOL: f64 = 0.01;
442	
443	/// When the warmup stretch settled: seconds from warmup start to
444	/// the first probe from which the floor stayed inside
445	/// [`SETTLE_TOL`] of the level warmup ended at. `None` when there
446	/// is nothing to measure (an empty stretch or a zero floor).
447	///
448	/// - **Why report it at all.** Once warmup deliberately spans the
449	///   ramp, the grade stops seeing the ramp — which is warmup
450	///   working, and would otherwise leave the report saying nothing
451	///   about a box that took a second to come up to speed. The
452	///   letter answers "was it settled when measurement started";
453	///   this answers "how long did that take", which is the number
454	///   the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo turns into a stopping rule.
455	/// - The settled level is the *tail window's* median floor
456	///   (`tail`), so it is the same reference the warmup grade is
457	///   scored against.
458	/// - The rule is "when did the floor last leave the band": the
459	///   settle time is the probe after the last one outside it, so
460	///   movement anywhere in the stretch is reflected, not just
461	///   movement a suffix median survives. A suffix-median rule was
462	///   tried first and read `settled 0.00s` on stretches whose own
463	///   `drift` signal graded F — a minority of moved probes never
464	///   shifts the median.
465	/// - "Outside the band" is asked of a [`SETTLE_WINDOW`]-probe
466	///   *median*, not of a probe. The letter is computed from
467	///   medians, so a per-probe rule disagrees with it: on a
468	///   bimodally-flickering 3900X floor, single probes leave a 1%
469	///   band constantly while every median the grade takes stays
470	///   put, and settle time read "never settled" beside a
471	///   drift/step of 0.00% A. A window median makes the two
472	///   answer the same question — a state the box actually held
473	///   for a while.
474	/// - A stretch still moving at its end reports [`Settle::Never`]
475	///   rather than a time. The time it would report is the last
476	///   probe's, which reads as "settled, just barely" — the exact
477	///   misreading of a box that never settled at all.
478	pub fn settle(warm: &[ProbeSummary], tail: &[ProbeSummary]) -> Option<Settle> {
479	    let tail_floors: Vec<f64> = tail.iter().map(|p| p.floor_q_ps as f64).collect();
480	    let level = median(&tail_floors)?;
481	    if level <= 0.0 {
482	        return None;
483	    }
484	    let windows = window_floors(warm);
485	    let last_out = windows
486	        .iter()
487	        .rposition(|&f| (f - level).abs() / level > SETTLE_TOL);
488	    match last_out {
489	        // The probe after the last excursion; no probe after it
490	        // means the stretch ended still moving.
491	        Some(i) => match warm.get(i + 1) {
492	            Some(p) => Some(Settle::At(p.t_start_s)),
493	            None => Some(Settle::Never),
494	        },
495	        None => warm.first().map(|p| Settle::At(p.t_start_s)),
496	    }
497	}

content.text:
Fix is in, installed, and the Todo is filed as #4 (`vc-x1 fix-todo` renumbered the rest). Your invocation now reads:

```
  run   warmup  env-run  worst   settle   mean
  1     A       A        A       2.25s    21.8 ns
  2     F       A        F       not      24.4 ns
  ...
  median settle: 3.69s (1 of 6 never settled)
```

The F run reports `not` rather than a number near the budget, and the times spread instead of pinning to the end.

**Respawn vs loop — the definitions.**

- **Respawn** (what it does today): the parent calls `Command::new(current_exe)` once per run. Each child is a fresh OS process — new address space, cold instruction and data caches, cold branch predictors, a fresh allocator arena, a new main thread — which does its own warm, measures, prints a report, and exits. The parent reads its stdout and parses the letters back out of the text.
- **Loop**: one process runs N rounds in sequence with sleeps between them. Process-local state persists across rounds — caches stay warm, the allocator keeps its arenas, the thread is the same one — and the results stay in memory as data rather than becoming text and being parsed back.

The distinction that matters is *what gets reset*, and it is narrower than the current module doc claims. Respawn resets process-local state. **Neither resets the machine.** The P-state, the thermal state, the uncore clock — the things the environment grade actually measures — belong to the box, and a fork doesn't touch them. What re-rolls those is the gap between runs and the duty cycle, both of which a loop controls just as well. So the stated reason for respawning ("in-process repeats would share warmed state") is really about process warmth, which isn't what the grade measures.

**Warmup at startup only** — that's what `-8` does: once per process, before the first bench, and every later bench inherits the machine state. No change needed.

**A bench that stalls, and the clock drops.** Real, and partly already handled:

- The run stretch already sees it. Seam probes run at every batch boundary, so a core that idles into a low P/C-state and ramps back shows up as `drift`/`step` on `env run:` — that's precisely the "the box moved under the measurement" signal, and it's why the seam probes exist rather than only warmup probes.
- `--blocks` already re-warms: each block sleeps, then steps unrecorded for 2 ms before measuring, so the post-wake ramp doesn't land in that block's samples.
- What's *not* handled is a stall inside a single continuous run — a blocking bench that parks long enough to drop state mid-batch. Today that gets reported (a step, at a stated time) and nothing re-warms.

My recommendation is to leave it reporting. Re-warming mid-run would mean the harness deciding a stall happened and inserting unrecorded work, which changes what the run measures — and for a blocking bench the stall *is* the workload. A round-trip that parks is genuinely slower than one that spins; erasing the ramp would flatter it. The place where a stall is a defect rather than a fact is warmup, which is the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo's territory: warm until the trailing window agrees, which naturally re-warms after any stall inside warmup.

*The plain version:* "respawn" means starting a whole new program for each test run; "loop" means one program doing the runs one after another. The difference is only whether the program's own memory is fresh — the CPU's speed state carries over either way, and that's the thing we're measuring, so looping would be fine and simpler. Warming up once at startup is what we now do. If a benchmark pauses long enough for the CPU to nod off mid-run, we'll say so in the report rather than secretly warming it back up, because for a benchmark that pauses on purpose, the pause is part of what you asked us to measure.

content.content:
### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal.
Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a
compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the
semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to
write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no
single replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker),
plus commit titles. It applies going forward; existing text
converts when touched. A code span is not exempt by itself.
Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this
section names them. A banned character doing a job is a use and
converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes `` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an
error message, an already-published commit title) is
transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether
or not it sits in a code span. It matters most for commit
titles: converting one stops it matching `git log --grep` and
breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
requires between a commit title, its chores header, and its
`## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

content.text:
Good instinct, and I think it's strictly better than the blacklist — for one reason that dominates the rest: **a blacklist can never be complete, and its failures are invisible.** `—`, `–`, `…`, `→` are the four you noticed. The ones you won't notice are U+00A0 non-breaking space (renders as a space, breaks greps and wraps), zero-width space, a Cyrillic `а` in an identifier, and the µ/μ pair — U+00B5 micro sign versus U+03BC Greek mu, visually identical, and this repo writes `µs` in several places. A whitelist closes the set: anything not explicitly allowed is out, including the characters nobody has thought of yet.

It also dissolves the scope ambiguity we just hit. "Durable text the bot writes" needed a judgment call about `.rs` doc comments; "bytes in a file" doesn't. One rule covers `.rs`, `.md`, `.toml` and needs no list of surfaces.

And it's one grep, so it can be enforced rather than remembered:

```
grep -PnR '[^\x09\x0A\x20-\x7E]' -- <paths>
```

That's the whole validator, and it reports file:line for anything that slips.

**On "maybe a few others" — my answer is zero others, and it's cheaper than it sounds**, because every legitimate need already has an ASCII spelling or an escape:

- `µs` becomes `us`, `±` becomes `+/-`, `≥`/`≤` become `>=`/`<=`, `≈` becomes `~`, `×` becomes `x` (which the code already uses in `BATCH_OVER_MULT x floor`).
- In Rust, anything genuinely needing a codepoint writes `\u{2026}` — the *file* stays ASCII while the *program* doesn't. That's a nice property: the constraint is on the source, not on the behavior.
- Transcribed external text (a pasted error message, a published commit title) is the one case the parked section explicitly exempts. Under a byte rule it can't be exempted invisibly, which I'd call a feature: either escape it, or note that it was transcribed and normalized.
- The real cost is a name — a citation to an author with an accent. Rare here, and a bibliography entry can carry the ASCII spelling with the original noted.

Start with zero exceptions and let a genuine need argue its way in. Loosening later is easy; tightening after exceptions accumulate is not — which is the same argument the parked section makes for why its own rule is absolute rather than a lean.

Two details worth deciding:

- **Tab.** I'd allow it only where a format demands it (nothing here does; Rust is spaces, Markdown tabs are hostile). Allowing it generally buys invisible inconsistency.
- **`\r`.** Ban outright rather than allow — CRLF has no business in this tree, and excluding it from the whitelist makes that automatic.

**How it relates to the parked branch:** the valuable half of `### Typeable punctuation only` isn't the ban list, it's the guidance that an em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that wasn't made — become a colon, sub-bullets, a comma, or two sentences. That survives intact. The ban list is what the byte rule replaces, and the scope paragraph collapses to a sentence. Since that section only exists on `punctuation-sweep`, this should be an edit to *that* branch rather than a second convention written on main — otherwise 0.23.1 lands a rule we've already superseded.

Suggested split: file it as a Todo against the parked branch, and separately note that `src/` has ~150 existing violations, so the sweep and the validator want to land together — a rule with no enforcement decays, and enforcement against an unswept tree fails on day one.

For `-8` right now, none of that changes what I owe you: convert the em dashes in my own additions (README, TODO, chores-05, and the new doc comments), and write the commit message in ASCII. Want me to do that pass now, or after you've finished reading the diff?

content.text:
Agreed on both, and the rule collapses to a single expression that says exactly what you described:

```
grep -PnR '[^\x09\x0A\x20-\x7E]' --include='*.rs' --include='*.md' .
```

Tab and newline allowed, `\r` excluded by simply not being in the set, everything above 0x7E out, and the `--include` list *is* the scope. No table of banned characters to maintain and no prose defining "durable text".

Three things I'd raise before it's written down:

**Tab in `.md` has one sharp edge.** rustfmt never emits tabs, so in `.rs` a tab can only appear inside a string or a doc comment, where it's merely invisible. In Markdown a leading tab is an indented code block — so a tab in a bullet continuation silently turns prose into a code block, and the rendered output changes without the source looking wrong. Allowing it is fine; it's just worth knowing that the one place tabs can bite is the file type where they're least likely to be intentional.

**"Source code" by extension may be drawing the line in the wrong place.** The distinction that actually matters is *authored by us* versus *generated or received*:

- `iiac-perf.toml.example` is documentation wearing a `.toml` extension — it's almost entirely prose comments explaining each key, and I added a paragraph to it this session. Under a `.rs`/`.md` scope it's exempt, though it's precisely the kind of durable prose the rule exists for.
- `Cargo.lock` and the generated completion YAML must be exempt no matter how the rule is phrased, because we don't author their bytes.
- `.claude/*.jsonl` is a journal of received text and is exempt under any framing.

So I'd suggest the scope read "files we author" with the extension list as its implementation — `*.rs`, `*.md`, and the `.toml` files we hand-write (`Cargo.toml`, `.vc-config.toml`, `iiac-perf.toml.example`), with generated files excluded by name. Same one-liner, one more `--include` and an exclusion or two.

**Commit messages aren't files.** The parked section's scope explicitly includes commit titles, and a rule stated as "bytes in a file" doesn't reach them. If the byte rule replaces the ban list, commit messages need their own clause — and the validator can check them via `jj log` output rather than a file scan. Worth keeping, since the commit-title case is the one with a real consequence: a converted title stops matching `git log --grep` against its chores header.

Also still true from before: this belongs as an edit to the parked `punctuation-sweep` branch, not a second convention on main, and the validator wants to land with a sweep of `src/`'s ~150 existing violations — a rule that fails on day one against its own tree teaches people to ignore it.

Shall I do the `-8` conversion pass now (my additions to README, TODO, chores-05, `iiac-perf.toml.example`, and the new doc comments), and write the commit message in ASCII? That's independent of where the convention finally gets written down.
