(intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very
short clauses or tight pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when
breaking would be more noise than signal.

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal.
Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a
compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the
semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to
write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no
single replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but
the spaces on both sides survive, so `## A — B` slugs to
`#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point
inbound links in the same commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker),
plus commit titles and everything under `src/`: doc comments,
inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is the
surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable
character costs more there than in prose. It applies going
forward; existing text
converts when touched. A code span is not exempt by itself.
Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this
section names them. A banned character doing a job is a use and
converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes `` `.expect(...)` ``.

error message, an already-published commit title) is
transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether
or not it sits in a code span. It matters most for commit
titles: converting one stops it matching `git log --grep` and

## Typeable punctuation only

Files we author contain only these bytes:

- `U+0009` tab
- `U+000A` newline
- `U+0020` through `U+007E`, printable ASCII

Everything else is banned, `U+000D` carriage return included.
The list is what is allowed, not what is forbidden, and that is
the whole point:

- **A banned list cannot be complete, and its misses are
  invisible.** The characters that cost the most are the ones
  nobody thinks to ban: `U+00A0` no-break space renders as a
  space while breaking greps and wrapping, `U+200B` zero-width
  space renders as nothing at all, and `U+00B5` micro sign and
  `U+03BC` Greek mu are indistinguishable on screen, so `us` gets
  spelled two ways that never match each other.
- **The rule is one command**, so it can be enforced rather than
  remembered:

  ```
  grep -PnR '[^\x09\x0A\x20-\x7E]' --include='*.rs' --include='*.md' .
  ```

- **The include list is the scope.** Nothing has to define
  "durable text" in prose or rule on whether doc comments count:
  a file is in the set or it is not.
- **`U+000D` is excluded rather than exempted**, which keeps CRLF
  out of the tree without a second rule.
- **Tab is allowed** because some formats require it. Note that a
  leading tab in Markdown is an indented code block, so a tab in
  a bullet continuation silently turns prose into code: allowed,
  but seldom what was meant.

Replacements are mechanical where the character stands for
itself: `...` for the ellipsis, `->` for the arrow, `+/-` for
plus-or-minus, `us` for microseconds, `>=`, `<=`, `~`, and `x`
for the multiplication sign. The dashes have no single
replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at one
  line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences.
  Often the aside should just go.

Converting a heading changes its slug, because the dash strips
while the spaces around it survive: the colon form of a heading
slugs one hyphen shorter (see
[Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point
inbound links in the same commit.

Out of scope, because we did not write the bytes:

- **Files we do not author**: generated output (`Cargo.lock`, a
  completion spec), transcripts, anything received rather than
  written.
- **String and character literals**, where a program must emit a
  byte we cannot type. In Rust `\u{2014}` keeps the file itself
  inside the rule and is preferred, but a literal is fine when
  the escape costs more than it saves.
- **Translated or otherwise international documentation**, which
  is out of scope by definition.

Name a character by codepoint (`U+2014`) rather than displaying
it. A banned-list rule has to print the characters it bans, and
"a specimen stays" is an exemption no validator can check, since
nothing distinguishes a specimen from a use. Naming them removes
the exemption and lets the one grep above be the whole check.

## Working Directory

Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
discuss with the user first, because losing track of cwd causes
subtle command failures downstream.

When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path,
usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
tool args also stay absolute; that's a tool-boundary constraint,
not a stylistic choice.

Run **one command per shell invocation**; don't bundle several
steps into a single compound script (`a && b; c`). Bundling hides
which step produced which output and makes a failure ambiguous;
executing one at a time keeps the details visible and reviewable.

inseparable pair where the join is the point.

`tmp/` at the repo root is the scratch area for temporary
files: parked notes, intermediate outputs, throwaway
scripts. It is gitignored (jj honors `.gitignore`), so
nothing in it can ride into a commit.

  it's on the project filesystem (fast moves, survives
  reboots), visible to both user and bot, and invisible to
  jj snapshots.
- Created on demand (`mkdir -p tmp`); the dir itself is
  never committed, so a fresh clone starts without it.

  can still use `/tmp`.

# iiac-perf comments on the unified AGENTS.md / cycle-protocol.md

Notes from the iiac-perf side toward one shared AGENTS.md and
cycle-protocol.md, written 2026-07-30 during the `0.23.0-8` rung
(`feat: warm the box once per process`). Companion to
[AGENTS-iiac-perf.md](AGENTS-iiac-perf.md), which is this repo's
AGENTS.md verbatim plus a new
[Typeable punctuation only](AGENTS-iiac-perf.md#typeable-punctuation-only)
section.

Each item below is an observation, the evidence behind it, and a
proposal. Evidence is from one long session, so treat the numbers
as one sample, not a study. Where we are guessing at a mechanism,
we say "we think".

## One command per shell invocation: the text is not the problem

The rule is already in all three files, near-verbatim
(`AGENTS.md:72`, `AGENTS-vc-x1.md:66`,
`AGENTS-iiac-perf.md:87`). Making it universal is a no-op. What
it needs is a reason it does not hold.

Measured over this session's journal, counting `Bash` tool calls
that joined steps with `&&` or `;`:

```
bash calls: 121   bundled: 73   (60%)
```

The rule was in context from the first turn. It still lost, 3
times in 5. We think the mechanism is that an agent pays a
visible cost per tool call (latency, turn count, transcript
length) and no visible cost for bundling until something fails,
so the incentive runs against the rule continuously while the
rule fires only at failure.

It also cost something real here. The cargo cycle was run as one
bundle, `fmt && clippy && test && install`, which is exactly the
shape the rule warns about: when the user asked "did you run the
pre-flight commands", neither of us could tell from the
transcript which stage had run against which version of the
tree. The answer turned out to be that `install` had run before
the version bump, so `0.23.0-7` was on `PATH` while the working
copy said `-8`. One command per invocation would have made that
a one-line answer instead of a re-run.

Proposal, in three parts:

- **Split the rule by effect, not by syntax.** The current
  phrasing bans a character (`&&`, `;`) and then carves out
  "a genuine pipeline" and "a tight, inseparable pair", which
  are judgment calls made in the moment by the party that wants
  to bundle. Effect is checkable:
  - **State-changing steps never bundle**: build, install,
    commit, push, file writes, anything that leaves the tree or
    the machine different. Each gets its own invocation so its
    output and exit status are attributable.
  - **Read-only inspection may bundle** when the parts are
    delimited (`grep A; echo ---; grep B`). This is most of the
    73 above, it costs nothing, and leaving it nominally banned
    is what trains the reader to treat the whole rule as
    advisory.
- **Enforce it.** A `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that rejects a
  command containing `&&` when any segment matches a
  state-changing verb list (`cargo install`, `cargo build`,
  `jj commit`, `jj git push`, `vc-x1 push`, `rm`, `mv`, `cp`,
  `sed -i`, `tee`) turns a rule that decays into one that
  cannot. A rule with no checker is a rule with a half-life.
- **Say what it buys, in the imperative.** "Bundling hides which
  step produced which output" is true and abstract. "You will
  not be able to answer 'which version did that install put on
  PATH'" is the same claim with a consequence attached.

## Typeable punctuation: allowed list, not banned list

`AGENTS-vc-x1.md:342` bans four characters. iiac-perf has the
same section parked on a branch (`punctuation-sweep`, to land as
`0.23.1`), so main here has not adopted it yet. The section in
[AGENTS-iiac-perf.md](AGENTS-iiac-perf.md#typeable-punctuation-only)
proposes the inverse: name the bytes that are allowed
(`U+0009`, `U+000A`, `U+0020` through `U+007E`) and ban
everything else.

Why the inversion matters, beyond taste:

- **A banned list cannot be complete.** The four listed are the
  ones a reader notices. The ones that cost are invisible:
  `U+00A0` no-break space, `U+200B` zero-width space, and the
  `U+00B5` / `U+03BC` pair that spells microseconds two
  indistinguishable ways. An allowed list catches all of them
  without naming any.
- **It makes the rule one command**, which is the difference
  between a convention and a check:
  `grep -PnR '[^\x09\x0A\x20-\x7E]' --include='*.rs' --include='*.md' .`
- **The include list is the scope**, which retires a paragraph.
  The current scope prose ("the same as Speculation marker, plus
  commit titles and everything under `src/`") had to be extended
  twice already, and it still left us arguing this session over
  whether `.rs` doc comments were durable text.
- **It removes an unenforceable carve-out.** "Naming the
  character is a specimen and stays" cannot be checked, since
  nothing distinguishes a specimen from a use. Naming characters
  by codepoint (`U+2014`) removes the exemption. Note the
  current sections cannot satisfy their own rule: 7 of the 11
  non-ASCII bytes left in `AGENTS-vc-x1.md` are its own
  specimens, and the other 4 are `<=` written as a glyph.

Carve-outs we think are genuinely needed, and no more: files we
do not author (generated, transcribed, received), string and
character literals where a program must emit an untypeable byte
(prefer `\u{2014}`, which keeps the file itself compliant), and
international documentation.

## Two rules that only bite when they are checked

Related to both items above, and worth stating once in the
unified file rather than per-rule: a convention with a checker
survives, and one without it decays into a thing the bot
apologizes for. Evidence from this session alone:

- `TODO.md` numbering has `vc-x1 validate-todo` and
  `vc-x1 fix-todo`. It stayed correct with no effort: adding an
  entry mid-list renumbered 24 others in one command.
- Punctuation has no checker. `src/` accumulated ~150 violations
  before anyone counted, and this session added 28 more before
  the user caught one by eye at `gauge.rs:488`.
- Intra-doc links have a checker that is not in the per-commit
  flow. A rename left three broken `[`settle_s`]` links that
  `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` passes clean;
  `cargo doc` reports them. They would have shipped.

Proposal: the unified AGENTS.md gains a short section listing
each convention and its checker, with "none" spelled out where
there is none. That list is then the backlog for
`vc-x1 validate-repo`.

## cycle-protocol.md: two gaps this session found

- **The validation step should include `cargo doc`.** The Rust
  cargo cycle is `fmt -> clippy -> test -> install`. Rustdoc
  lints (broken intra-doc links, unclosed HTML tags in doc
  comments) are reported by none of those. `cargo doc --no-deps
  --document-private-items` catches them and takes seconds. This
  repo currently carries 8 such warnings, all pre-existing.
- **The version bump must precede the validation step, and the
  protocol should say so.** Preparation says "bump the
  version-of-record" and the per-commit flow says "validate",
  but nothing orders the bump against `cargo install` within a
  Work commit. Installing before the bump puts the previous
  version on `PATH` while the tree claims the new one, which is
  precisely what the version-of-record exists to prevent
  ("useful for confirming you're running the version you're
  testing"). It happened here and the user caught it. One
  sentence in [Per-commit flow] fixes it: the bump is step 0,
  before the work, so every artifact built during the commit
  carries the version the commit will ship.

## Drift between the two AGENTS.md files

Structurally they are the same document: diffing headings gives
four differences, three of which are punctuation. Bodies differ
in 103 hunks, nearly all wording. Two are worth a decision:

- **`--scope` flag values disagree.** `AGENTS-iiac-perf.md` says
  `--scope=code|bot|code,bot`; `AGENTS-vc-x1.md` says
  `--scope=work|bot|work,bot`. The shipped tool (`vc-x1 0.71.0`)
  says `code|bot|code,bot`, so vc-x1's own AGENTS.md is
  describing a rename that has not landed. We think a unified
  file should avoid naming flag values it cannot verify, or the
  sync process should regenerate them from `--help`.
- **`ochid:` multiplicity.** iiac-perf ties multiple `ochid:`
  trailers to the merge non-ff close-out specifically; vc-x1
  generalizes to "when a single push publishes several work-repo
  commits". vc-x1's is the better statement: it is about the
  push, not about the shape.

## One structural wart, cheap to fix

All three files contain a literal `## refactor: extract config
loader` heading. It is an *example* chores header quoted inside
the Chores conventions section, but being a real `##` it lands
in the document outline, in every `grep '^## '`, and in any
generated TOC, between "Chores conventions" and "Cycle
Protocol". Fencing it (or demoting it to inline code) removes a
phantom section from the shared file.

## Open questions

- Does the unified file keep a per-project appendix, or do
  project-specific bits (this repo's `// OK:` unwrap convention,
  its band-label vocabulary) live in the project's own file with
  the shared one included by reference? Today's duplication is
  what let the two copies drift.
- Is `tmp/` (scratch files) universal or project-local? Both
  projects have it; the template does not.
- Should the punctuation checker run over commit messages as
  well as files? The rule as bytes-in-files does not reach them,
  and the commit-title case is the one with a consequence: a
  converted title stops matching `git log --grep` against its
  chores header.

- **Split the rule by effect, not by syntax.** The current
  phrasing bans a character (`&&`, `;`) and then carves out
  "a genuine pipeline" and "a tight, inseparable pair", which
  are judgment calls made in the moment by the party that wants
  to bundle. Effect is checkable:
  - **State-changing steps never bundle**: build, install,
    commit, push, file writes, anything that leaves the tree or
    the machine different. Each gets its own invocation so its
    output and exit status are attributable.
  - **Read-only inspection may bundle** when the parts are
    delimited (`grep A; echo ---; grep B`). This is most of the
    73 above, it costs nothing, and leaving it nominally banned
    is what trains the reader to treat the whole rule as
    advisory.
- **Enforce it.** A `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that rejects a
  command containing `&&` when any segment matches a
  state-changing verb list (`cargo install`, `cargo build`,
  `jj commit`, `jj git push`, `vc-x1 push`, `rm`, `mv`, `cp`,
  `sed -i`, `tee`) turns a rule that decays into one that
  cannot. A rule with no checker is a rule with a half-life.
- **Say what it buys, in the imperative.** "Bundling hides which
  step produced which output" is true and abstract. "You will
  not be able to answer 'which version did that install put on
  PATH'" is the same claim with a consequence attached.

## Typeable punctuation: allowed list, not banned list

`AGENTS-vc-x1.md:342` bans four characters. iiac-perf has the
same section parked on a branch (`punctuation-sweep`, to land as
`0.23.1`), so main here has not adopted it yet. The section in
[AGENTS-iiac-perf.md](AGENTS-iiac-perf.md#typeable-punctuation-only)
proposes the inverse: name the bytes that are allowed
(`U+0009`, `U+000A`, `U+0020` through `U+007E`) and ban
everything else.

Why the inversion matters, beyond taste:

- **A banned list cannot be complete.** The four listed are the
  ones a reader notices. The ones that cost are invisible:
  `U+00A0` no-break space, `U+200B` zero-width space, and the
  `U+00B5` / `U+03BC` pair that spells microseconds two
  indistinguishable ways. An allowed list catches all of them
  without naming any.
- **It makes the rule one command**, which is the difference
  between a convention and a check:
  `grep -PnR '[^\x09\x0A\x20-\x7E]' --include='*.rs' --include='*.md' .`
- **The include list is the scope**, which retires a paragraph.
  The current scope prose ("the same as Speculation marker, plus
  commit titles and everything under `src/`") had to be extended
  twice already, and it still left us arguing this session over
  whether `.rs` doc comments were durable text.
- **It removes an unenforceable carve-out.** "Naming the
  character is a specimen and stays" cannot be checked, since
  nothing distinguishes a specimen from a use. Naming characters
  by codepoint (`U+2014`) removes the exemption. Note the
  current sections cannot satisfy their own rule: 7 of the 11
  non-ASCII bytes left in `AGENTS-vc-x1.md` are its own
  specimens, and the other 4 are `<=` written as a glyph.

Carve-outs we think are genuinely needed, and no more: files we
do not author (generated, transcribed, received), string and
character literals where a program must emit an untypeable byte
(prefer `\u{2014}`, which keeps the file itself compliant), and
international documentation.

## Two rules that only bite when they are checked

Related to both items above, and worth stating once in the
unified file rather than per-rule: a convention with a checker
survives, and one without it decays into a thing the bot
apologizes for. Evidence from this session alone:

- `TODO.md` numbering has `vc-x1 validate-todo` and
  `vc-x1 fix-todo`. It stayed correct with no effort: adding an
  entry mid-list renumbered 24 others in one command.
- Punctuation has no checker. `src/` accumulated ~150 violations
  before anyone counted, and this session added 28 more before
  the user caught one by eye at `gauge.rs:488`.
- Intra-doc links have a checker that is not in the per-commit
  flow. A rename left three broken `[`settle_s`]` links that
  `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` passes clean;
  `cargo doc` reports them. They would have shipped.

Proposal: the unified AGENTS.md gains a short section listing
each convention and its checker, with "none" spelled out where
there is none. That list is then the backlog for
`vc-x1 validate-repo`.

## cycle-protocol.md: two gaps this session found

- **The validation step should include `cargo doc`.** The Rust
  cargo cycle is `fmt -> clippy -> test -> install`. Rustdoc
  lints (broken intra-doc links, unclosed HTML tags in doc
  comments) are reported by none of those. `cargo doc --no-deps
  --document-private-items` catches them and takes seconds. This
  repo currently carries 8 such warnings, all pre-existing.
- **The version bump must precede the validation step, and the
  protocol should say so.** Preparation says "bump the
  version-of-record" and the per-commit flow says "validate",
  but nothing orders the bump against `cargo install` within a
  Work commit. Installing before the bump puts the previous
  version on `PATH` while the tree claims the new one, which is
  precisely what the version-of-record exists to prevent
  ("useful for confirming you're running the version you're
  testing"). It happened here and the user caught it. One
  sentence in [Per-commit flow] fixes it: the bump is step 0,
  before the work, so every artifact built during the commit
  carries the version the commit will ship.

## Drift between the two AGENTS.md files

Structurally they are the same document: diffing headings gives
four differences, three of which are punctuation. Bodies differ
in 103 hunks, nearly all wording. Two are worth a decision:

- **`--scope` flag values disagree.** `AGENTS-iiac-perf.md` says
  `--scope=code|bot|code,bot`; `AGENTS-vc-x1.md` says
  `--scope=work|bot|work,bot`. The shipped tool (`vc-x1 0.71.0`)
  says `code|bot|code,bot`, so vc-x1's own AGENTS.md is
  describing a rename that has not landed. We think a unified
  file should avoid naming flag values it cannot verify, or the
  sync process should regenerate them from `--help`.
- **`ochid:` multiplicity.** iiac-perf ties multiple `ochid:`
  trailers to the merge non-ff close-out specifically; vc-x1
  generalizes to "when a single push publishes several work-repo
  commits". vc-x1's is the better statement: it is about the
  push, not about the shape.

## One structural wart, cheap to fix

All three files contain a literal `## refactor: extract config
loader` heading. It is an *example* chores header quoted inside
the Chores conventions section, but being a real `##` it lands
in the document outline, in every `grep '^## '`, and in any
generated TOC, between "Chores conventions" and "Cycle
Protocol". Fencing it (or demoting it to inline code) removes a
phantom section from the shared file.

## Open questions

- Does the unified file keep a per-project appendix, or do
  project-specific bits (this repo's `// OK:` unwrap convention,
  its band-label vocabulary) live in the project's own file with
  the shared one included by reference? Today's duplication is
  what let the two copies drift.
- Is `tmp/` (scratch files) universal or project-local? Both
  projects have it; the template does not.
- Should the punctuation checker run over commit messages as
  well as files? The rule as bytes-in-files does not reach them,
  and the commit-title case is the one with a consequence: a
  converted title stops matching `git log --grep` against its
  chores header.

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>

### Outcome

The cycle set out to stop subtracting an ill-defined overhead and
to grade the run rather than the room. Both landed, and the
report changed shape in the process.

- **Reported values are raw.** `overhead.rs`, the constants, the
  adjusted column and the `calibrate` command are gone, and
  nothing estimates a quantity that cancels in same-harness A/B.
- **Two grades, from two populations.** `run:` scores the
  batches the run itself produced; `env` scores the box from
  micro-probes that never touch the bench. An F on one beside an
  A on the other is a true and useful statement, which the single
  calibration letter could not make.
- **The box has a selftest.** `qualify-environment` respawns this
  binary, reads the environment stretches, and exits nonzero when
  the machine is not fit to measure on. It needs no toolchain on
  the box under test.
- **Startup is warmed once per process**, so the first bench no
  longer reports a cold machine's numbers, and the warmup row
  reports how long settling took.

What the cycle deliberately did not fix, each with an owner:

- **The 3900X's bistable floor.** Measured 2026-07-30: a 1.5 s
  warm absorbs the startup ramp, but the ~10% shift recurs at
  arbitrary times, and a 3.5 s warm still left 2 of 4 runs
  moving. No warm length reaches it; replication (`--blocks`) is
  the answer, and the box correctly fails `qualify-environment`.
- **A convergence rule for warmup.** The "Dynamic startup warmup"
  Todo owns it, and inherits the probe series and the settle
  statistic this cycle built as its input.
- **The report's grade block is verbose**: 85 grade lines on an
  `all` sweep. The columns Todo owns the reformat.
- **The selftest still runs a bench** it does not need, since
  every number in its table comes from the probe series. Todo #4
  owns removing it.
"""
s = s.replace(a, outcome + a)
open(p,'w').write(s)

# Notes

This directory contains various notes and documentation related to the project.
Each file is organized by topic for easy reference.

By default there are the chores-NN.md files in
[chores/](chores). Chores are general notes about tasks;
short term tasks and their status live at the repo root in
[../TODO.md](../TODO.md). The chores-NN files are numbered
in sequence; the highest-numbered file is the active one,
older ones are closed.

Durable design analyses (measurement theory, error models,
decisions that outlive a cycle) live in
[design.md](design.md). Measurement results that outlive a
cycle (e.g. the thread-placement map) live in their own topic
files — [placement-map.md](placement-map.md). Known defects
awaiting a fix live in [bugs.md](bugs.md); durable
machine/session ops facts in [ops.md](ops.md). For users new
to jj see [jj-tips.md](jj-tips.md).

Examples chore file:
```
# Chores-01.md

General maintenance tasks and considerations for the project see other files for
more specific topics. A chore in a chores file provides quick information on the
how and why of a particular chore.

## Create a binary that lists jj info

This binary should list the changeID, commitID, and description title
and using `jj-lib`
```

## Workflow and conventions

Bot-facing workflow and conventions live in
[`../AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md):

- [Notes file conventions](../AGENTS.md#notes-file-conventions)
  — Todo format, Reference numbering, Notes references
